name: Ajivika (position-entry)
evidence_basis: Opponent reconstruction, supplemented by inscriptional attestation of the community.
own_corpus_survival: No securely identified Ajivika text survives.
dates_notes: This is a community and position entry, not an author entry. The lower bound follows the placement of Makkhali Gosala among the early sramana teachers in Buddhist and Jaina sources; the third-century BCE Barabar cave dedications of Asoka independently attest an Ajivika community. Neither body of evidence permits a secure foundation date or a continuous institutional history.
core_thesis: Ajivika designates an early Indian ascetic community whose doctrines are known chiefly from Buddhist and Jaina reports, not from an Ajivika-authored corpus. Those reports consistently associate the tradition with niyati, a strong account of necessity or determinism: the course of beings is not ultimately altered by moral effort, ascetic practice, or ritual action. This makes the Ajivika position an important challenge to accounts of karmic efficacy and deliberate liberation. The scope and exact formulation of the doctrine remain uncertain because the reports are polemical and differ in emphasis; this entry therefore records a recoverable historical position rather than a reconstructed system in full.
reception_notes: The principal literary evidence is the Buddhist Samannaphala Sutta and Jaina accounts of Gosala and the Ajivikas; both preserve rival descriptions rather than self-testimony. Asoka's Barabar cave inscriptions establish that an Ajivika community received imperial patronage in the third century BCE, but they do not expound doctrine. No text should be presented as an Ajivika primary source unless its provenance is independently established.
